title: Dictionary Mutability
concept: Dictionaries are mutable - adding, modifying, and removing keys changes the same object!

content.code:
person = {"name": "Alice", "age": 25}
print(f"id = {id(person)}")

person["age"] = 26
person["city"] = "Seoul"
print(f"After changes: {person}")
print(f"id = {id(person)}")

ref = person
ref["name"] = "Bob"
print(f"person: {person}")

steps.title: Create a dictionary
steps.explanation:
`person = {"name": "Alice", "age": 25}` creates a dictionary object.

**Dictionaries are MUTABLE** - like lists, they can be modified in place.

steps.title: Note the id
steps.explanation:
Let's remember this id.

For mutable objects, the id stays the same after modification!

steps.title: Modify existing key
steps.explanation:
`person["age"] = 26` modifies the value for key "age".

**In-place modification** - same dictionary object!

steps.title: Add new key
steps.explanation:
`person["city"] = "Seoul"` adds a new key-value pair.

**Still the same object!** No new dictionary created.

steps.title: SAME id!
steps.explanation:
**The id is unchanged!**

This proves all modifications happened to the same object.

**Like lists:** `d[key] = value` modifies in place.

steps.title: Create alias
steps.explanation:
`ref = person` creates an **alias**.

Now `ref` and `person` point to the SAME dictionary!

**Same trap as lists!**

steps.title: Modify through alias
steps.explanation:
`ref["name"] = "Bob"` modifies the shared dictionary.

Since both names point to the same object...

steps.title: person ALSO changed!
steps.explanation:
**Both see the change!**

`person: {'name': 'Bob', 'age': 26, 'city': 'Seoul'}`

**Dictionaries have the same aliasing trap as lists!**

Use `.copy()` or `dict()` to avoid this.

quiz.question: What creates an independent copy of dict d?
quiz.explanation: Both d.copy() and dict(d) create shallow copies. e = d just creates an alias. For nested dicts, use copy.deepcopy().

misconceptions.wrong: d2 = d1 creates a copy of the dictionary
misconceptions.correct: d2 = d1 creates an alias - both point to same dict
misconceptions.why: Assignment binds names to objects. It never copies objects.

misconceptions.correct: Dictionary keys must be immutable (strings, numbers, tuples)
misconceptions.why: Mutable objects can't be hashed consistently, so they can't be keys.

keyTakeaway: Dictionaries are MUTABLE like lists. d[key] = value modifies in place. Watch out for aliasing!
